scenarios.title: Manage the last minute with a lead
scenarios.objective: Compare possession options under a stated late-game objective.
scenarios.briefing: Navy leads by one with 48 seconds remaining. YOU have controlled possession near the neutral-zone side boards. The coach asks for a controlled play that preserves defensive support; this does not mean every forward option is forbidden. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The briefing states the lead and remaining time; they are not inferred from the rink.

Gold 1’s pressure toward the carrier

scenarios.title: Create another attempt while trailing late
scenarios.objective: Assess a late attacking choice without declaring a guaranteed scoring play.
scenarios.briefing: Navy trails by one with 32 seconds left and has five skaters on the ice. YOU control at the puck-side point. F1 is near the net, F2 is across the high slot and D2 is the other high player. The goalie remains in net; no extra attacker is assumed. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.

options.text: Check the remaining clock and immediate lanes

scenarios.title: Attack a power-play entry before the setup forms
scenarios.objective: Recognize an available rush option without assuming the unit must first arrange a formation.
scenarios.briefing: Navy has five skaters against four. YOU carry a controlled wide entry, F2 offers middle support and F3 trails. The coach permits a rush chance if it is clearly available; the unit is not required to establish an in-zone formation first. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.

questions.prompt: What does the stated team instruction permit?

options.text: A clearly available rush chance before a set formation
Only a complete formation before any chance
A guaranteed goal because of five-on-four

questions.explanation: The briefing explicitly permits an early rush option while retaining a lane check.

questions.prompt: Which two cues help judge that option?

options.text: A requirement to stop solely because it is a power play
F2’s readiness and route
Gold 1 and Gold 2’s coverage of the entry

questions.explanation: The local read still matters on special teams; the numerical advantage is not an answer key.

questions.prompt: Arrange an entry read under this instruction.

options.text: Read the entry defenders
Compare the immediate chance with retained possession
Attack or settle according to the available picture

questions.explanation: Both attacking and settling may be reasonable under different cues.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a carrier angle connecting the wide entry to middle support.
questions.explanation: The example changes the relation to F2 and Gold 1. It does not validate a passing window or skating race.

questions.prompt: Gold 2 closes F2 and Gold 1 contains your lane. What could be useful?

options.text: Treat the power play as over
Protect possession and look for the trailing support
Force the old rush pass because the coach permitted a chance

questions.explanation: Permission to attack does not require forcing a chance after its routes close.

questions.prompt: How is “allowed to score from the rush” different from “must shoot immediately”?
questions.explanation: The first preserves choices based on the defenders; the second ignores whether a useful chance actually exists.

questions.prompt: What should YOU say before the permitted rush entry?

options.text: The lane is conditional; F2 and F3 show me the next option
The instruction requires an immediate shot
Gold’s pressure shape stays the same after the entry angle changes

questions.explanation: The call keeps permission separate from a forced action and names support.

questions.prompt: Which two checks belong before using the rush?

options.text: Gold 1 and Gold 2 pressure
F2 or F3 reachability
The power-play label alone

questions.explanation: Pressure and support decide whether the permitted entry is usable.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a carrier angle that connects wide entry and middle support.
questions.explanation: This point changes the entry line while retaining both receivers.

questions.prompt: Gold closes both visible support lanes. What should YOU reconsider?
questions.explanation: Protect the puck or reset instead of forcing the permitted rush. Permission remains conditional on a reachable lane.

scenarios.title: Protect the backdoor during a penalty-kill rotation
scenarios.objective: Track a low weak-side threat under a declared penalty-kill responsibility.
scenarios.briefing: Navy kills four-on-five. Gold 1 controls at the puck-side half wall, Gold 2 is below the goal line and Gold 3 waits across the low slot. YOU are the weak-side low defender. This drill assigns YOU the weak-side low threat until a teammate confirms an exchange. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: Gold 3 is in the weak-side low slot while Gold 1 carries at the puck-side half wall.

scenarios.title: Join the second wave only after checking possession
scenarios.objective: Assess an offensive activation while keeping a stated covering defender.
scenarios.briefing: F1 has recovered the puck and carries into the neutral zone. YOU are the supporting defender; D2 stays deeper by agreement. F2 is ahead and Gold 3 is recovering near YOU. The drill permits an activation only after secure possession and available support are checked. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.

findings.issue: q7 changes the explicit 48-second situation to one minute left.
findings.evidence: The briefing states Navy leads by one with 48 seconds remaining; q7 asks “with one minute left,” which is a different game state and can change the risk read.
findings.recommendedChange: Replace q7 prompt with “What should YOU communicate with 48 seconds left?” Keep the conditional option and explanation, or say “under a minute” if exact precision is not intended. Rehash q7.

findings.issue: q7 and q8 refer to D1 as the deeper cover, but the scene explicitly assigns that role to D2.
findings.evidence: The briefing says D2 stays deeper by agreement. q7 says “D1 is behind me,” and q8 asks whether D1 leaves the deeper cover; D1 is not the assigned cover in this setup.
findings.recommendedChange: Replace D1 with D2 in q7 and q8, preserving the rest of each question: q7 “F1 has control and D2 is behind me; call if either changes”; q8 option b “D2 leaves the deeper cover.” Rehash q7/q8.

rows.reason: The repaired prompt uses the briefing's actual 48-second clock and keeps a clear forward lane conditional. It avoids the false claim that a one-goal lead bans every forward option; the alternative answers are plausible late-game misreads.

The repair names F1 as the actual puck carrier and D2 as the agreed deeper cover, matching both briefing and puck owner. The request to call if either changes makes the activation conditional rather than treating the communication as proof of control.

The two keyed changes directly remove the drill's stated prerequisites: F1 no longer has secure possession or D2 no longer supplies deeper cover. F2 staying wide is a credible non-trigger because the prompt does not make F2's width the activation condition.

The reference at (0,4.5) is behind F1 at (3,0) in Navy's attacking direction and is separated from F3 at (8,7). Feedback preserves the required D2 cover and Gold 3 recovery read, so the position is an example lane rather than a mandatory route.

The sequence teaches late-game risk management as a contextual scan: confirm time/score/support, compare pressure, then choose and communicate the next support job. q2 names the constraints and q5 proves a forward pass can still fit, avoiding a generic never-attack rule.
